# Shell basics {#sec-shell-basics}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Say what the shell does with a command line before a program runs,
   and tell a shell builtin from a program.
2. Move around the filesystem with absolute and relative paths, `~`,
   `.`, and `..`, and check where you are with `pwd`.
3. Create, copy, move, rename, link, and delete files and folders, and
   avoid the commands' silent overwrites and permanent deletes.
4. Predict what a wildcard matches, quote names with spaces or special
   characters, and use tab completion and history to type less.
5. Find files with `find`, and look inside files with `less`, `head`,
   `tail`, and `file`.
:::

## Why the command line {#sec-shell-basics-why}

This chapter opens Part II, six chapters on the Linux command line.
That is a large share of a bioinformatics book to spend on typing
commands, so first, the reason.

**Real work runs on Linux machines that you reach through a
terminal.** A university cluster such as Nova or SCINet's Ceres runs
Linux. You log in with `ssh`, and what you get is a prompt, not a
desktop. Companies, and labs without a cluster, rent Linux servers in
the cloud (@sec-cloud) and reach them the same way. Your laptop is for
editing, small tests, and writing up. The data and the long jobs live
on those machines (@sec-orientation-where). @sec-orientation-linux
explained why they run Linux; this part teaches you to work on them.

The command line also suits the work itself, not only the machines it
runs on (@tbl-why-command-line).

: Why bioinformatics is done at the command line. {#tbl-why-command-line}

| Reason | What it means in practice |
|:-------|:--------------------------|
| The tools are command-line programs | aligners, `samtools`, `seqkit`, and nf-core pipelines all run from a prompt; most have no point-and-click version |
| It scales | one wildcard runs the same command on 2 files or 2,000 (@sec-shell-basics-wildcards) |
| It leaves a record | a command is text: paste it into `NOTEBOOK.md`, rerun it, save it in a script, or send it to a colleague. Clicks leave nothing to rerun. |
| It runs while you are away | the cluster's scheduler runs your script after you log out (@sec-hpc-slurm); it cannot click buttons for you |
| It works over any connection | a terminal sends only text, so it stays usable from home or over a slow link (@sec-working-remotely) |

**Why bash.** The *shell* is the program that reads what you type
(@sec-shell-basics-shell). There are several shells. Bash is the
default on nearly every Linux system and cluster, cluster job scripts
are usually bash scripts, and tools' install instructions assume it.
So the book uses bash everywhere, including on a Mac, where you made
it your shell in @sec-orientation. Learn it once, and the same
commands work on your laptop, the cluster, and a cloud server.

Part II builds up to running a real job on a cluster, one chapter at a
time (@tbl-part2-roadmap).

: What each chapter of Part II adds. {#tbl-part2-roadmap}

| Chapter | What you can do afterwards |
|:--------|:---------------------------|
| @sec-shell-basics (this one) | move around, manage files safely, match names with wildcards, look inside files |
| @sec-text-tools | filter, count, and summarise text files by joining small tools with pipes |
| @sec-linux-system | read permissions, set `PATH`, watch and stop processes, check disk use |
| @sec-shell-scripts | save commands as a script that reruns the same way every time |
| @sec-working-remotely | log in with SSH keys, keep work running when the connection drops, move data safely |
| @sec-hpc-slurm | submit scripts as jobs to a cluster's scheduler, with the resources they need |

## What this chapter does {#sec-shell-basics-intro}

You have already run about thirty shell commands in Part I, mostly by
copying them: `mkdir -p … && cd …`, `ls -lh`, `cat`, `head`, `mv`,
`cp`, `ln -s`, `chmod`, `touch`. Each time the book said "explained in
Part II". This is that explanation. Once you know what each part of a
command does, you can change it, predict what it will do, and spot the
one character that is wrong.

The chapter covers what the shell does with a line before any program
runs; how to move around the filesystem; how to copy, move, link, and
delete without losing files; wildcards and quoting; `find`; looking
inside files of any size; and recalling earlier commands instead of
retyping them. Pipes and redirection (`|`, `>`) are @sec-text-tools;
permissions, `PATH`, and your shell's settings are @sec-linux-system;
variables and scripts are @sec-shell-scripts. A few supplied commands
here contain a `|`; copy those as they are.

Commands run on your laptop. In the book's project, `~/bioinf-computing`,
you only **look** at files in this chapter; the one thing you write
there is your own notes in `NOTEBOOK.md`, as in @sec-organizing-projects
and @sec-getting-help. Everything that creates, moves, or deletes
happens in a scratch folder, `~/bioinf-computing-ch05`, so a mistake
cannot touch the project.

**Build the practice folder.** Paste the block below into your terminal
in one go. It makes `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/`, a stand-in for
the kind of folder a former lab member leaves behind: reads in three
run folders, one with spaces in its name; plots and a counts file; two
sample tables; a stray temporary file; and a link that points nowhere.
@sec-text-tools, @sec-linux-system, and @sec-shell-scripts reuse this
folder, so keep it.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05
mkdir ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share && {
mkdir run1 run2 "Run 3 final" analysis meta
printf '@A.%s\nACGTACGTAC\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 | gzip > run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
printf '@A.%s\nGTACGTACGT\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 | gzip > run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
printf '@B.%s\nACGTACGTAC\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 | gzip > run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
printf '@B.%s\nGTACGTACGT\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 | gzip > run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
cp run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp
printf '@C.%s\nACGTACGTAC\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 4 | gzip > "Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
printf '@C.%s\nGTACGTACGT\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 4 | gzip > "Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz"
touch "analysis/plot 1.png" "analysis/plot 2.png"
seq 1 1000 > "analysis/counts FINAL.txt"
rows=(sample run_folder condition reads
  sample_C "Run 3 final" treated 12
  sample_A run1 control 9
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_E run5 treated 105
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_D run4 control 8)
printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${rows[@]}" > meta/samples.tsv
printf '%s,%s,%s,%s\r\n' "${rows[@]}" > meta/samples_from_excel.csv
printf 'Reads from runs 1-3. Ask Sam about run 3.\n' > notes.txt
printf 'colour=on\n' > .old_settings
touch -d 2025-03-01 notes.txt .old_settings
ln -s /no/such/genome ref
printf 'pwd\nls data/raw\n' > ../where.sh
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05 && ls -A share
}
```

```{.console}
 .old_settings   analysis   meta   notes.txt   ref  'Run 3 final'   run1   run2
```

It is safe to paste without understanding it yet. This chapter explains
`mkdir`, `cd`, `cp`, `touch`, and `ln -s`; `printf`, `gzip`, and the
`|` come in @sec-text-tools, and the `rows=(…)` list in
@sec-shell-scripts. The read files are real, tiny gzipped FASTQ files
(2, 3, and 4 reads for samples A, B, and C), so the tools you use on
them behave as on real data. On a Mac, `touch -d` needs the GNU tools
from @sec-orientation's setup.

Pasting the block a second time is safe: `mkdir` stops with `File
exists` and nothing else runs, so it cannot undo changes you made. To
rebuild the folder on purpose, rename the old one first and paste again:
`mv ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share_old`.
The book never deletes a scratch folder for you.

## What a shell is {#sec-shell-basics-shell}

Type these, one at a time:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~
ls
lss
type cd
type mkdir
```

```{.console}
bioinf-computing       bioinf-computing-ch03  bioinf-computing-ch05
bioinf-computing-ch01  bioinf-computing-ch04  bioinf-shared
bash: lss: command not found
cd is a shell builtin
mkdir is /usr/bin/mkdir
```

Your home folder will hold other things too. `lss` gives the message
from @tbl-common-errors: no program has that name. (Ubuntu may add a
suggestion: `Command 'lss' not found, did you mean …`.) `type` asks bash
what a name is: `cd` is part of bash itself, while `mkdir` is a program
stored in a file. On a Mac after @sec-orientation's setup, `type mkdir`
shows the GNU copy, `/usr/local/opt/coreutils/libexec/gnubin/mkdir` or
a path under `/opt/homebrew`. (Try `type ls` too: on many systems it
says `ls is aliased to …`. Aliases are @sec-linux-system.)

**Now name the parts.** The **terminal** is the window. The **shell**
is the program inside it that reads what you type and starts other
programs; this book's shell is **bash**. A **command** is either a
program (`ls`, `mkdir`, `seqkit`) or a **builtin**, part of bash
itself (`cd`, `pwd`, `echo`, `type`, `history`). `cd` has to be a
builtin: a separate program runs as its own process, and changing *its*
folder would leave your shell where it was.

Every line follows the shape you met in @sec-getting-help's usage
lines: the command first, then its **options** (`-l`, `--help`), then
its **arguments**, usually names of files or folders. Whatever the
command, bash first does the same work on the line (@fig-shell-steps):

1. It **reads the line into words**, at spaces, but respecting quotes
   and backslashes: `"Run 3 final"` stays one word.
2. It **expands** `~`, wildcards such as `*`, and `$…` where quoting
   allows.
3. It **removes the quote characters** themselves.
4. It **finds the command** and starts it with the resulting
   **arguments**.

::: {#fig-shell-steps}
{{< svg ../figures/shell-steps.svg >}}

What bash does with a line before `ls` starts. The quoted name stays
one word, the unquoted pattern is replaced by the matching names, the
quotes are removed, and `ls` receives four arguments. Use *Next* to
step through.
:::

Quoting decides what happens in steps 1 and 2. A file name produced by
a wildcard is one argument even if it contains spaces, as
@sec-shell-basics-wildcards shows. (Bash calls something else "word
splitting": splitting the result of a `$…` expansion, which is
@sec-shell-scripts. Step 1 is just reading the line.) This is the frame
for the whole chapter: quoting and wildcards are steps 1–3, and how
bash finds a program in step 4 (`PATH`) is @sec-linux-system. The
[Bash manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Shell-Expansions.html)
gives the full order of expansions, for later.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Before any program starts, bash reads your line into words (respecting
quotes), expands `~`, wildcards, and `$…` where quoting allows, and
removes the quotes. The program gets only the resulting arguments.
Most surprises in this chapter come from that step.
:::

**Bash, not zsh.** A new Mac's default shell is zsh, which is similar
but not the same. @sec-orientation made bash your shell on every system,
because clusters use it. Check:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "$BASH_VERSION"
```

```{.console}
5.3.15(1)-release
```

Any version from 4 up is fine; Ubuntu 24.04 has 5.2, and a cluster may
have an older one (Nova had 5.1 in November 2026). If nothing prints, you are not in bash: go back to
@sec-orientation.

**The prompt.** A prompt such as `you@laptop:~/bioinf-computing$` tells
you who you are (`you`), which machine you are on (`laptop`), and which
folder you are in (`~/bioinf-computing`), then `$`: ready. Clusters set
theirs up for you; the host name tells you whether you are on a login
node (@sec-hpc-slurm). Yours may look different; @sec-linux-system shows
how to change it.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Why can't `cd` be a separate program, like `mkdir`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
A program runs as its own process. If it changed folder, only its own
folder would change, and your shell would stay where it was. `type cd`
says `cd is a shell builtin`.
:::
:::

## The filesystem tree and paths {#sec-shell-basics-paths}

Predict what each `pwd` prints, then run the lines one at a time:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pwd
cd ~/bioinf-computing
pwd
ls
cd data/raw
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd ../..
pwd
cd -
cd
pwd
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Output

```{.console}
/home/you
/home/you/bioinf-computing
data  NOTEBOOK.md  pixi.lock  README.md  src
logs  notes.txt    pixi.toml  results
/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/raw
/home/you/bioinf-computing/data
/home/you
/home/you/bioinf-computing/data
/home/you
```

`/home/you` is your own home folder: `/Users/you` on a Mac. `cd -`
printed a folder because it goes back to the previous one and says
where that is. `cd` alone went home.
:::

@fig-cd-steps shows the same moves on the folder tree.

::: {#fig-cd-steps}
{{< svg ../figures/cd-steps.svg >}}

The `cd` sequence above, one step per command. The outlined folder is
the current working directory; the terminal strip shows what `pwd`
prints there.
:::

**Now name the parts** (@fig-filesystem-tree). Every file on the
machine sits in **one tree** that starts at `/`, the **root**. Your
**home folder** is one branch of it, `/home/you`, and `~` is short for
it. A **path** names a place in the tree:

- An **absolute path** starts at the root, with `/`:
  `/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/meta`. It means the same thing from
  anywhere. A path starting with `~` is absolute too, since bash turns
  `~` into `/home/you` (step 2 above).
- A **relative path** starts from where you are, the **current working
  directory** that `pwd` prints. From `data/raw`, `../meta` means "up
  one folder, then into `meta`".
- `.` is the current folder and `..` the one above it.

::: {#fig-filesystem-tree}
{{< svg ../figures/filesystem-tree.svg >}}

One tree from `/`. The book's project and the scratch folder are in your
home folder; programs live under `/usr/bin`; a cluster adds project and
scratch areas outside home. The absolute path to `meta` starts at the
root; the relative path from `raw` goes up one folder (`..`) and down
again. On a Mac, home is `/Users/you`.
:::

: Path shortcuts, from inside `~/bioinf-computing/data/raw`.
{#tbl-path-shortcuts}

| Symbol | Means | Example | `pwd` afterwards |
|:-------|:------|:--------|:-----------------|
| `/` (at the start) | the root: an absolute path | `cd /home/you/bioinf-computing` | `/home/you/bioinf-computing` |
| `~` | your home folder | `cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05` | `/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05` |
| `.` | the current folder | `ls .` (same as `ls`) | unchanged |
| `..` | the folder above | `cd ../..` | `/home/you/bioinf-computing` |
| `-` (with `cd`) | the previous folder | `cd -` | wherever you were before |
| nothing (with `cd`) | home | `cd` | `/home/you` |

Where your home folder is depends on the system (@tbl-home-by-system).

: Home folders and other places you will work. {#tbl-home-by-system}

| System | Home folder | Other places you will work | Note |
|:-------|:------------|:---------------------------|:-----|
| Linux | `/home/you` | — | |
| Windows (WSL2) | `/home/you`, inside Linux | your Windows files at `/mnt/c/Users/…` | keep work in the Linux home (@sec-orientation) |
| macOS | `/Users/you` | — | |
| Cluster | `/home/<user>`, small | project and scratch areas: `/project/…` and `/90daydata/…` on SCINet, `/work/…` on Nova | @sec-cluster-sites, @sec-hpc-slurm |

Names are case-sensitive, as @sec-organizing-projects said: `Data` and
`data` are different folders on Linux and on clusters.

**Relative to what?** A relative path always means "from where I am
now", even inside a script. The setup block made a two-line script,
`~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh`, that prints the current folder and
lists `data/raw`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh
cd ~/bioinf-computing
bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh
cd ~
bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh
```

```{.console}
pwd
ls data/raw
/home/you/bioinf-computing
checksums.md5  SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
/home/you
ls: cannot access 'data/raw': No such file or directory
```

The same script, run by the same absolute path, gives two results,
because `data/raw` is looked up from the folder you ran it in. From `~`
it looked for `~/data/raw`, which does not exist. @sec-getting-help's
wrong-folder case was related but failed earlier: `pixi run` itself
looks for `pixi.toml` in the current folder and the folders above it,
and found none.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "A relative path is relative to the script that contains it"
**Reality.** It is relative to the current working directory of the
shell that runs the command, wherever the script is stored. Run project
scripts from the project folder, as the book does, or `cd` there first.
:::

**Errors you will meet:**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd nowhere
cd ~/bioinf-computing/README.md
```

```{.console}
bash: cd: nowhere: No such file or directory
bash: cd: /home/you/bioinf-computing/README.md: Not a directory
```

Note that the second message shows `~` already expanded: `cd` never saw
the `~`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Press Tab
Type `cd ~/bioi` and press {{< kbd Tab >}}. Bash completes as far as
the name is certain, here `~/bioinf-`, because several folders start
that way (`bioinf-computing…`, `bioinf-shared`). Press {{< kbd Tab >}}
twice to list the choices, type a few more letters, and press it again.
Tab saves typing and catches typos: more in @sec-shell-basics-wildcards.
:::

**On a cluster.** The same commands work on a login node. Log in as in
@sec-orientation and run:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
pwd
echo "$HOME"
type ls
```

On Nova (captured November 2026; `<user>` is your user name):

```{.console}
/home/<user>
/home/<user>
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
```

`pwd` prints your **cluster** home: a different machine with a
different home folder, which holds none of your laptop's files (`ls`
there shows only what you have put on the cluster). `type ls` shows the
alias from @sec-shell-basics-shell, which makes `ls` colour its output. `~` always means the home of the machine you are on. Project and
scratch areas are @sec-hpc-slurm and @sec-cluster-sites; moving files
between machines is @sec-working-remotely.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You are in `~/bioinf-computing/data/raw`. Give a
relative and an absolute path to `samples.tsv` in `data/meta`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Relative: `../meta/samples.tsv`. Absolute:
`~/bioinf-computing/data/meta/samples.tsv`, or
`/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/meta/samples.tsv` written out.
:::
:::

## Looking around: `ls` and its options {#sec-shell-basics-ls}

In the project folder, try each option:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
ls -a
ls -F
ls -lh data/raw
ls -ld data/raw
ls -lt logs
```

```{.console}
.   .pixi  logs         notes.txt  pixi.toml  results
..  data   NOTEBOOK.md  pixi.lock  README.md  src
data/  NOTEBOOK.md  pixi.lock  README.md  src/
logs/  notes.txt    pixi.toml  results/
total 4.3M
-r--r--r-- 1 you you  112 Nov 17 11:22 checksums.md5
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2.2M Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2.2M Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
dr-xr-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 11:22 data/raw
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 369 Nov 17 12:28 01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122821_jlSC.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 399 Nov 17 12:24 01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
```

Your dates, sizes of logs, and log names will differ, and you may have
more logs. What each option did:

- **`-a`** (all) shows names starting with a dot. `.pixi` is the hidden
  folder where @sec-book-setup's environment lives: do not edit it by
  hand; `pixi install` rebuilds it. `.` and `..` are the current and the
  parent folder. A leading dot **hides** a name by convention; it does
  not protect it. (`-A` shows hidden names without `.` and `..`.)
- **`-F`** adds `/` after folders (and `@` after links, `*` after
  programs).
- **`-l`** (long) gives one line per file, and **`-h`** prints sizes in
  human units (`2.2M` instead of `2239317`). Options combine: `-lh` is
  `-l -h`, as in @sec-getting-help.
- **`-d`** lists a folder itself instead of its contents
  (@sec-organizing-projects used it to check `data/raw` was locked).
- **`-t`** sorts by time, newest first: the quickest way to find the
  latest log.

With names as arguments, `ls` lists only those. Most systems colour
names by type in the terminal (folders blue, links cyan); the book shows
output without colour. When a name contains a space, GNU `ls` puts it in
quotes, as in `'Run 3 final'` in the setup block's output: the quotes
show where the name starts and ends and are not part of it.

**Read one long line** with @fig-ls-long.

::: {#fig-ls-long}
{{< svg ../figures/ls-long.svg >}}

Two `ls -l` lines, field by field: a read-only FASTQ file and the
`data/ref` link. The first character is the type; the permissions are
@sec-linux-system. A link's size is the length of the path it holds.
:::

A folder's size in `ls -l` (`4096` above) is the size of its list of
names, not of what is inside; `du` measures that (@sec-linux-system).

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `ls` shows nothing in a folder, but the disk-usage
tool says the folder holds 2 GB. What do you try first?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`ls -a`: the space is probably in hidden files or folders, names that
start with a dot, such as `.pixi`.
:::
:::

## Creating, copying, moving, and deleting {#sec-shell-basics-files}

Work in a new `practice` folder inside the scratch folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice
mkdir notes
mkdir p/q
mkdir -p p/q # <1>
touch notes/todo.txt # <2>
cp notes/todo.txt notes/todo_copy.txt
cp notes backup
cp -r notes backup # <3>
mv backup/todo_copy.txt backup/done.txt # <4>
mv backup old_notes
ls
```
1. `-p` makes every missing folder on the way, and is quiet if the
   folder exists.
2. `touch` makes an empty file (or updates the time of an existing one).
3. `-r` (recursive) copies a folder and everything inside it.
4. `mv` renames a file here, and renames a folder on the next line: one
   command, two jobs, moving and renaming.

```{.console}
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘p/q’: No such file or directory
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'notes'
notes  old_notes  p
```

`mkdir p/q` failed because `p` did not exist; `-p` makes both. `cp`
without `-r` refuses a folder. `mv old new` moves a file or folder to a
new name, or into a folder if `new` is an existing folder:
`mv backup/done.txt notes/` would move the file into `notes`.

Now the ways to delete:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rmdir p
rm p
rm -r p # <1>
ls
```
1. `rm -r` removes a folder and everything in it.

```{.console}
rmdir: failed to remove 'p': Directory not empty
rm: cannot remove 'p': Is a directory
notes  old_notes
```

`rmdir` removes only empty folders, which makes it the safe choice when
you think a folder is empty. `rm` removes files, and with `-r`, folders
and everything in them.

### Three surprises

**`cp` and `mv` overwrite without asking.** Make two small files and
copy one over the other (`>` writes a command's output into a file, as
in @sec-orientation; @sec-text-tools explains it):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "version 1" > old.txt
echo "version 2" > new.txt
cp new.txt old.txt
cat old.txt
echo "version 3" > newer.txt
mv newer.txt old.txt
cat old.txt
ls
```

```{.console}
version 2
version 3
new.txt  notes  old_notes  old.txt
```

No question, no warning: `version 1` is gone, then `version 2`. `-i`
(interactive) asks first, and `-n` (no-clobber) never overwrites:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "version 4" > new.txt
cp -n new.txt old.txt
cat old.txt
cp -i new.txt old.txt
```

```{.console}
version 3
cp: overwrite 'old.txt'? n
```

`cp -n` skipped the copy without a message; `cp -i` asked, and `n`
kept the old file.

**`rm` has no trash folder and no undo.** A file removed with `rm` is
gone at once; nothing on the command line puts it back. `rm -i` asks
before each file. `rm -r` on the wrong folder is the classic disaster.

**A trailing slash matters for links.** @sec-organizing-projects showed
that `rm -r data/ref/` follows the link and deletes the shared files.
Remove a link with `unlink name` or `rm name`: no slash, no `-r`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: no undo
`rm` deletes for good, and `cp` and `mv` overwrite silently. Before you
delete, list exactly the names the command will get, with
`ls -d -- <the same names>`. Keep raw data read-only and backed up
(@sec-organizing-projects): those are the only undo.
:::

### The safe habit: preview, then delete

Go to the practice tree and list what a wildcard would hand to `rm`
(wildcards are explained in @sec-shell-basics-wildcards; `run*` means
"names starting with `run`"):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
ls run*
ls -d -- run*
```

```{.console}
run1:
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz  sample_A_R2.fastq.gz

run2:
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz  sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp  sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
run1  run2
```

Plain `ls run*` showed what is **inside** the two folders. But
`rm -r run*` would get the folders themselves, `run1` and `run2`, and
`ls -d -- run*` lists exactly those. So the habit is:

1. Run `ls -d --` with the names or pattern you mean to delete.
2. If the list is right, press {{< kbd Up >}}, change `ls -d` to
   `rm -i` (@sec-shell-basics-history shows the editing keys), and run
   it.

`--` means "no more options after this". Quotes keep a name with spaces
as one argument, but they do not stop a name that starts with `-` from
being read as an option. Try it on a throw-away file named `-n`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice
touch -- -n
rm -n
rm -i -- -n
```

```{.console}
rm: invalid option -- 'n'
Try 'rm ./-n' to remove the file '-n'.
Try 'rm --help' for more information.
rm: remove regular empty file '-n'? y
```

`rm` itself suggests the other way out: `./-n` starts with `.`, so it
cannot be an option. That was your first real deletion, of a file you
made a minute ago, with `-i` asking first.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "Deleted files go to a trash folder I can restore from"
**Reality.** `rm` removes the name at once. There is no trash on the
command line; only backups, or snapshots that some sites keep of some
storage (@sec-cluster-sites), can bring a file back. Ask before you
count on snapshots.
:::

More habits, one line each:

- Never run `rm -rf` on a path built from a variable or a wildcard you
  have not previewed (variables are @sec-shell-scripts).
- Keep raw data read-only: in @sec-organizing-projects, `chmod a-w`
  turned a slip into `Permission denied`.
- The book does not suggest making `rm` always ask (an alias for
  `rm -i`): the habit stops protecting you the day you work on a machine
  without it.

@tbl-file-commands collects the commands.

::: {.wide-table}
: Commands that create, copy, move, link, and delete, and what they do
without asking. {#tbl-file-commands}

| Command | Does | Overwrites or deletes without asking? | Safer form | Undo? |
|:--------|:-----|:--------------------------------------|:-----------|:------|
| `mkdir -p a/b` | makes folders, with any missing parents | no | — | `rmdir` |
| `touch f` | makes an empty file, or updates its time | no | — | `rm f` |
| `cp a b` | copies a file | **yes**, if `b` exists | `cp -i`, `cp -n` | none |
| `cp -r d e` | copies a folder and its contents | **yes**, files inside `e` | `cp -ri` | none |
| `mv a b` | moves or renames | **yes**, if `b` exists | `mv -i`, `mv -n` | move back, if nothing was overwritten |
| `rm f` | deletes a file | **yes**: that is its job | `ls -d -- f` first; `rm -i` | backups only |
| `rm -r d` | deletes a folder and everything in it | **yes** | `ls -d -- d` first; `rm -ri` | backups only |
| `rmdir d` | deletes an **empty** folder | no: refuses if not empty | — | `mkdir d` |
| `ln -s target name` | makes a symbolic link | no existing file is replaced, but if `name` is a folder or a link to one, the new link goes **inside** it; `ln -sT` refuses instead | — | `unlink name` |
| `unlink name` | removes one link or file | **yes** | no trailing slash | make the link again |
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `mv results_new.tsv results.tsv`, and
`results.tsv` already existed. What happened to it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
It is gone: replaced without a question. `mv -i` would have asked and
`mv -n` would have refused; now only a backup brings it back.
:::
:::

## Symbolic links, revisited {#sec-shell-basics-links}

@sec-organizing-projects made `data/ref`, a link to the shared reference
folder. Here are four ways to ask where a link points:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
ls -l data/ref
readlink data/ref
readlink -f data/ref
realpath data/raw/../ref
```

```{.console}
lrwxrwxrwx 1 you you 53 Nov 17 11:22 data/ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
/home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
/home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
/home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
```

`readlink` prints the path the link **stores**; `readlink -f` and
`realpath` print where it finally **leads**, after following every link
and every `..`. Here they agree because the link stores an absolute
path. (For reference: you will rarely need `readlink -f` and
`realpath`, but they are the tools for "where does this really go?")

**A broken link.** The practice folder's `ref` points to a path that
does not exist:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
ls -l ref
cat ref
find . -xtype l
```

```{.console}
lrwxrwxrwx 1 you you 15 Nov 17 11:40 ref -> /no/such/genome
cat: ref: No such file or directory
./ref
```

`ls -l` still shows the link and its arrow (often in red), but anything
that opens it fails with `No such file or directory`, although `ref` is
right there in the listing. `find . -xtype l` lists broken links; it
comes back in @sec-shell-basics-find.

**Relative targets.** A link can store an absolute path or a relative
one, and a relative one is read from **the link's own folder**, not from
the folder where you ran `ln -s`. This is the most common way to make a
broken link (@fig-link-targets). Try it from `share`, making links in a
new folder `tidy` next to it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
mkdir -p ../tidy
ln -s run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz
ln -s ../share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/right.fastq.gz
file -h ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz ../tidy/right.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz: broken symbolic link to run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
../tidy/right.fastq.gz: symbolic link to ../share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
```

`wrong.fastq.gz` stores `run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz`, which is read from
`tidy/`, where there is no `run1`. `right.fastq.gz` stores a path that
goes up from `tidy/` and into `share/`. (`file` names the kind of thing
a path is, more in @sec-shell-basics-viewing; `-h` makes it describe
the link itself instead of following it, which Linux does by default
but a Mac does not.) Remove both with
`unlink`, which removes only the links:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
unlink ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz
unlink ../tidy/right.fastq.gz
```

::: {#fig-link-targets}
{{< svg ../figures/link-targets.svg >}}

A relative link target is read from the folder the link is in. Both
commands were run in `share/`, but both links live in `tidy/`, so
`run1/…` leads nowhere, while `../share/run1/…` reaches the file.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: a relative target is read from the link's folder
`ln -s run1/x.fastq.gz ../tidy/x.fastq.gz` stores `run1/x.fastq.gz`,
which is looked up from `tidy/`, not from where you ran the command.
Use an absolute target, or write the path as seen from the link's
folder.
:::

When to use which (@tbl-link-targets): absolute targets for shared lab
data and references, as in @sec-organizing-projects; relative targets
inside one project that you might move or copy as a whole. In
`ln -s target name`, the target comes first, as the source does in
`cp source destination`. **Hard links** (`ln` without `-s`) also exist;
this book does not use them.

: Absolute and relative link targets. {#tbl-link-targets}

| Target written as | Read from | Still works if you move the link? | Still works if you move the target? | Use for |
|:------------------|:----------|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------|:--------|
| absolute, `/home/you/…` or `~/…` | the root | yes | no | shared data and references |
| relative, `../share/…` | the link's own folder | only if the target moves with it | only if the link moves with it | links inside one project |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** In `~/proj/data/` you run
`ln -s raw/x.fq.gz ~/proj/results/x.fq.gz`. Does the link work?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No. The link is in `~/proj/results/`, so its target `raw/x.fq.gz` is
looked up there, and there is no `results/raw/`. Use
`../data/raw/x.fq.gz` or an absolute path.
:::
:::

## Wildcards, quoting, and tab completion {#sec-shell-basics-wildcards}

**A prediction round first.** Go to `run1` in the practice folder.
`ls` shows two files, `sample_A_R1.fastq.gz` and
`sample_A_R2.fastq.gz`. For each line, write down what `echo` will print
(it prints its arguments), then run it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1
echo *
echo *.fastq.gz
echo *_R1*
echo sample_?_R1.fastq.gz
echo *.fq.gz
```

Then one level up, in `share`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ..
echo *
echo .*
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Output

```{.console}
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
*.fq.gz
analysis meta notes.txt ref Run 3 final run1 run2
.old_settings
```

`*` matches any characters, including none; `?` matches exactly one.
`*.fq.gz` matched nothing, so it came out unchanged. `*` skipped
`.old_settings`, and `.*` found only it. (Bash before 5.2, such as
Nova's 5.1, also lists `.` and `..` for `.*`.)
:::

**Now name it.** `echo` did not do any matching. **Bash replaces an
unquoted pattern with the matching names before the command starts**
(called *globbing*, or filename expansion). The program receives a list
of names and never sees the `*`. When nothing matches, bash's default is
to pass the pattern on unchanged (changing that default is
@sec-shell-scripts). That explains @sec-getting-help's case 2,
`[ERRO] stat data/raw/*.fq.gz: no such file or directory`: seqkit was
handed the literal `data/raw/*.fq.gz` and looked for a file with that
name. `ls` does the same:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls *.fq.gz
```

```{.console}
ls: cannot access '*.fq.gz': No such file or directory
```

@fig-glob-expansion shows all three cases.

::: {#fig-glob-expansion}
{{< svg ../figures/glob-expansion.svg >}}

Who matches a pattern. Unquoted, bash matches it against the files and
the program gets the names; with no match, the program gets the pattern
itself. Quoted, the pattern reaches the program unchanged, which is what
`find -name` wants.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "The program reads the `*` and finds the matching files itself"
**Reality.** For an unquoted pattern, bash does the matching first, and
the program gets names, or the unchanged pattern when nothing matches.
Only a quoted pattern reaches the program, which some programs, such
as `find -name`, want.
:::

**One argument per name, spaces included.** `echo` joins its arguments
with spaces, so it cannot show where one ends and the next begins. In
`share/analysis`, `plot 1.png` is one name, but `echo` makes it look like
two. `printf '<%s>\n'` prints each argument on its own line, between
`<` and `>`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
echo analysis/*
printf '<%s>\n' analysis/*
```

```{.console}
analysis/counts FINAL.txt analysis/plot 1.png analysis/plot 2.png
<analysis/counts FINAL.txt>
<analysis/plot 1.png>
<analysis/plot 2.png>
```

Three arguments, spaces kept: a name that comes from a wildcard is not
split again. That is why `ls analysis/*` handles these names fine, and
why `echo` is only a quick preview for simple names like the ones in
`run1`. To see the exact list a command would get, use `ls -d --` or
`printf '<%s>\n'`.

**Patterns.** @tbl-glob-patterns lists the ones you need. Brace
expansion looks similar but is different: it **makes** words, whether
or not files exist.

::: {.wide-table}
: Wildcard patterns, tried in `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share` (before
Exercise 3 tidies it). {#tbl-glob-patterns}

| Pattern | Matches | Example | Result |
|:--------|:--------|:--------|:-------|
| `*` | any characters, including none (not a leading `.`) | `echo run1/*` | `run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz` |
| `?` | exactly one character | `echo run?` | `run1 run2` |
| `[12]` | one of the listed characters | `echo run[12]/*_R1*` | `run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp` |
| `[!1]` | one character **not** listed | `echo run[!1]` | `run2` |
| `{A,B}` | brace expansion: makes each word, files or not | `echo sample_{A,B}_R1.fastq.gz` | `sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_B_R1.fastq.gz` |
| `{01..03}` | brace expansion: a range | `echo sample_{01..03}` | `sample_01 sample_02 sample_03` |
:::

Note the `[12]` row: `*_R1*` also matched the `.tmp` copy, because `*`
at the end matches `.fastq.gz.tmp` too. Patterns match **file names**,
not what is inside files (that is `grep`, @sec-text-tools), and they are
not regular expressions, which @sec-text-tools also covers. Brace
ranges are for reference; you will meet them again in loops
(@sec-shell-scripts).

**Programs that match patterns themselves.** Compare these two in
`share`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls *.fastq.gz
find . -name '*.fastq.gz'
```

```{.console}
ls: cannot access '*.fastq.gz': No such file or directory
./run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
./run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
./run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
./run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
```

`share` itself holds no `.fastq.gz` file, so bash passed `*.fastq.gz`
to `ls` unchanged. In the `find` line the quotes stop bash, so `find`
receives the `*` **on purpose** and matches it against every name in
every folder below. Your order may differ from this one.

### Quoting

Step 1 of @fig-shell-steps reads a line into words at spaces. So a name
with a space, typed plainly, becomes two arguments:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls analysis/plot 1.png
```

```{.console}
ls: cannot access 'analysis/plot': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '1.png': No such file or directory
```

Three ways to keep it one word, all of which work:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls "analysis/plot 1.png"
ls 'analysis/plot 1.png'
ls analysis/plot\ 1.png
```

The backslash form is what {{< kbd Tab >}} inserts for you. Double and
single quotes differ in one way that matters later: inside double
quotes bash still expands `$…` (variables, @sec-shell-scripts), and
inside single quotes it expands nothing. Quoting also turns off
wildcards and `~` (@tbl-quoting):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls "run1/*.fastq.gz"
ls "~/bioinf-computing"
```

```{.console}
ls: cannot access 'run1/*.fastq.gz': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '~/bioinf-computing': No such file or directory
```

The first looked for a file literally named `*.fastq.gz`. In the second,
`~` was not expanded, so the path is **relative**: a folder literally
named `~` inside the current folder, then `bioinf-computing` inside
that (the `/` still separates folders). Leave `~` outside the quotes,
or use `$HOME`, which double quotes do expand:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls ~/"bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final"
ls "$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final"
```

```{.console}
sample_C_R1.fq.gz  sample_C_R2.fq.gz
sample_C_R1.fq.gz  sample_C_R2.fq.gz
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `~` and wildcards inside quotes
`"~/data"` is a relative path: a folder literally named `~`, then `data`
inside it. Write `~/"My Data"` or `"$HOME/My Data"`. And `"*.fastq.gz"`
is the name `*.fastq.gz`, not a pattern.
:::

: What each kind of quoting keeps and expands. {#tbl-quoting}

| Form | Example | Spaces kept in one word? | `*` expanded? | `~` expanded? | `$…` expanded? |
|:-----|:--------|:-------------------------|:--------------|:--------------|:---------------|
| none | `ls plot 1.png` | no | yes | yes, at the start of a word | yes |
| double quotes | `ls "plot 1.png"` | yes | no | no | yes |
| single quotes | `ls 'plot 1.png'` | yes | no | no | no |
| backslash | `ls plot\ 1.png` | yes, for that character | not for an escaped `\*` | not for an escaped `\~` | not for an escaped `\$` |

Curly quotes copied from a PDF or a word processor (`“…”`, `‘…’`) are
not quotes to bash: they become part of the name, the same trap as
@sec-getting-help's en dash.

### Tab completion

{{< kbd Tab >}} completes as far as the name is unique; a second
{{< kbd Tab >}} lists the choices. It completes command names and paths,
and with the bash-completion package (installed on most Linux systems)
often options too. It is also a **typo detector**: if Tab will not
complete a name you are sure of, check with `ls`. It would have flagged
@sec-getting-help's `SRR6357070_l` at once. Treat it as a clue, not
proof: a prefix may match several names, permissions can get in the
way, and completion differs between commands.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Bash expands an unquoted wildcard; the program sees the matching names,
each as one argument. No match means the pattern is passed on as it is.
Quote a pattern when the program should match it itself (`find -name`).
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** In a folder with no `.bam` files you run `ls *.bam`.
What does `ls` receive, and what does it print?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The literal word `*.bam`, because nothing matched. It prints
`ls: cannot access '*.bam': No such file or directory`.
:::
:::

### Why careful names pay off

Experienced users name files `2026-11-17_read_counts.tsv` rather than
`Read Counts (final).txt`. This is not a matter of taste. On the
command line, names are typed, matched by wildcards, and split into
words, not clicked. The practice tree is messy on purpose:
`Run 3 final` breaks three of the naming rules in @tbl-file-names at
once (a space, a capital letter, and the vague word "final"). This
chapter has made you pay for each one. @tbl-name-costs gathers the
costs in one place.

: What each naming rule from @sec-organizing-projects saved you in this
chapter. {#tbl-name-costs}

| Rule | What breaking it cost here |
|:-----|:---------------------------|
| No spaces | `Run 3 final` needed quotes in every `cd`, `ls`, and `ln -s`; `echo` could not show where the name ended; `ls` printed it inside quotes |
| One case, lowercase | `run?` and `run*` missed `Run 3 final`; Tab completion is case-sensitive, so `cd ru` then {{< kbd Tab >}} never offers it |
| Only letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` | `*`, `?`, and `[ ]` match names; `$` expands; `( )`, `;`, `&`, `\|`, `<`, and `>` split or redirect commands. `ls Final FINAL (2).txt` stops with ``syntax error near unexpected token `('`` |
| Never start a name with `-` | `rm -n` read the file name as an option, so you needed `--` or `./-n` |
| Start with `.` only for hidden files | `ls` and `*` skip `.old_settings`; you see it only with `ls -a` |

**What about `CamelCase` or `MyData`?** Capital letters work, and
nothing breaks the first time you use them. The cost comes later. You
have to remember which letters were capitals every time you type a
name or press Tab. On Linux and the cluster, `MyData` and `mydata` can
sit side by side as two folders. On a Mac or in a Windows folder they
are the same name, so copying a project between them can overwrite one
with the other. All lowercase removes the question. Join words with
`_` (`read_counts.tsv`), and use `-` inside a single part, such as a
date or a version (`2026-11-17`, `R64-1-1`), as @tbl-file-names does.
For code, prefer `_`: Python cannot `import` a file named with a
hyphen, such as `count-reads.py` (@sec-python-essentials).

Two kinds of names keep their capitals. IDs from an archive or a
sample sheet stay exactly as given (`SRR6357070`, `WT_REP1`), so they
still match the records. A few files are capitalized by long
convention so that people and tools find them first: `README.md`,
`LICENSE`, `Makefile`, and your `NOTEBOOK.md`.

## Finding files with `find` {#sec-shell-basics-find}

`find` walks down a folder tree and prints every name that passes its
tests. Start with no tests:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05
find share
```

```{.console}
share
share/ref
share/analysis
share/analysis/plot 1.png
share/analysis/plot 2.png
share/analysis/counts FINAL.txt
share/notes.txt
share/meta
share/meta/samples.tsv
share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv
share/run2
share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp
share/.old_settings
share/run1
share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share/Run 3 final
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
```

Everything, hidden files included, in the order `find` meets it (yours
may differ). Now add tests:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
find share -name "*.fastq.gz"
find share -type l
find share -iname "*final*"
find share -maxdepth 1 -type f
```

```{.console}
share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share/ref
share/analysis/counts FINAL.txt
share/Run 3 final
share/notes.txt
share/.old_settings
```

`-name` matched the pattern against each name (not the folders above
it), and missed the `.fq.gz` files in `Run 3 final`. `-type l` found the
link; `-type f` means ordinary files and `-type d` folders. `-iname`
ignores upper and lower case, so `*final*` matched `FINAL` and `final`.
`-maxdepth 1` stopped `find` from going into subfolders. To find all
six read files, accept either ending:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
find share -type f \( -name "*.fastq.gz" -o -name "*.fq.gz" \)
```

```{.console}
share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
```

**The structure** is `find <where> <tests> [action]`:

- Tests written next to each other must **all** be true (an implicit
  AND): `-type f -name "*.tmp"` means "an ordinary file **and** named
  `*.tmp`".
- `-o` means OR, and `\( … \)` groups. The backslashes stop bash from
  reading the parentheses itself; the spaces around them are needed.
  Without the group, `-type f -name A -o -name B` means "(file and A) or
  B".
- The default **action** is to print each name.

Two tests for reference, useful on real data:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
find share -size +1k
find share -mtime +30
```

```{.console}
share/analysis/counts FINAL.txt
share/notes.txt
share/.old_settings
```

`-size +1k` means larger than 1 kilobyte: only the counts file, since
the toy FASTQ files are under 50 bytes each. On a `.gz` file, `-size`
measures the compressed file. `-mtime +30` means last changed more than
30 days ago: the two files the setup block back-dated to 2025-03-01.
`-mtime -1` would find files changed in the last day.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: quote the pattern after `find -name`
Unquoted, bash expands the pattern first (@sec-shell-basics-wildcards),
and `find` gets file names instead of the pattern. It can fail, or worse,
run and miss files.
:::

Both cases, on throw-away files:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice/findtest/deep
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice/findtest
touch a_1.fastq.gz a_2.fastq.gz deep/b_1.fastq.gz
find . -name *.fastq.gz
rm -i -- a_2.fastq.gz
find . -name *.fastq.gz
find . -name "*.fastq.gz"
```

```{.console}
find: paths must precede expression: `a_2.fastq.gz'
find: possible unquoted pattern after predicate `-name'?
rm: remove regular empty file 'a_2.fastq.gz'? y
./a_1.fastq.gz
./deep/b_1.fastq.gz
./a_1.fastq.gz
```

With two matches in the current folder, bash turned the command into
`find . -name a_1.fastq.gz a_2.fastq.gz`, and `find` objected (helpfully
guessing why). With one match, it became `find . -name a_1.fastq.gz`:
no error, and `deep/b_1.fastq.gz` silently missed. That is the worse
case, @sec-getting-help's lesson that no error does not mean a correct
result. Quoted, the last line found both.

@tbl-find-tests sums up the parts.

::: {.wide-table}
: The parts of a `find` command used in this book. {#tbl-find-tests}

| Part | Meaning | Example |
|:-----|:--------|:--------|
| `-name "pat"` | the name matches a quoted pattern | `-name "*.fastq.gz"` |
| `-iname "pat"` | the same, ignoring case | `-iname "*final*"` |
| `-type f` / `d` / `l` | ordinary file / folder / link | `-type f` |
| `-xtype l` | a broken link (GNU `find`) | `find . -xtype l` |
| `-maxdepth N` | go at most N levels down | `-maxdepth 1` |
| `-size +N` (reference) | larger than N (`k`, `M`, `G`) | `-size +1G` |
| `-mtime +N` / `-N` (reference) | changed more / less than N days ago | `-mtime -1` |
| next to each other | AND: all must be true | `-type f -name "*.tmp"` |
| `-o` | OR | `-name "*.fq.gz" -o -name "*.fastq.gz"` |
| `\( … \)` | group | `-type f \( … -o … \)` |
| (no action) | print each name (the default) | |
| `-exec`, `-delete` | actions: run a command on each, delete each | not used here (below) |
:::

**Where you will use it.** Finding where a pipeline wrote its outputs
(@sec-nf-core); counting your files when a cluster limits how many you
may have, with `find … -type f | wc -l` (@sec-hpc-slurm; the `|` is
@sec-text-tools); and finding broken links, as in Exercise 3.

`-exec` and `-delete` are **actions**, not tests, and this chapter does
not use them. `-delete` in particular is unforgiving: what it deletes
depends on where it sits in the expression (placed before the tests, it
deletes everything `find` reaches), it turns off printing, and it changes
the order of the search ([GNU findutils
manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/manual/)).
Clean-up here uses `unlink` and `rm -i`.

On a Mac, `-xtype` and `-printf` (used in Exercise 3) need GNU `find`,
which @sec-orientation's setup installed; GNU and BSD tools are compared
in @sec-linux-system. You may also meet `locate`, which searches a
prebuilt index: fast, but missing on most clusters and often out of
date.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Why is `find . -name *.fastq.gz` wrong even when it
seems to work?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Bash may expand the pattern first. With exactly one match in the current
folder, `find` looks only for that one name and misses the rest, with no
error.
:::
:::

## Looking inside files {#sec-shell-basics-viewing}

In the project, start with a short file, then the start and end of
longer ones:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
cat data/meta/samples.tsv
head -n 3 logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
tail -n 3 logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
```

Use your own log's name: `ls -t logs` lists them newest first, and
{{< kbd Tab >}} completes the name.

```{.console}
sample	run	geo_sample	condition	replicate
WT_REP1	SRR6357070	GSM2879618	wild_type	1
started:  2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
```

`cat` prints the whole file: fine for two lines. `head -n 3` prints the
first 3 lines and `tail -n 3` the last 3 (10 if you leave out `-n`).
`head` reads only the start of a file, so it is instant even on 100 GB.

**`less`** lets you move around a file of any length:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
less logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
less data/ref/README.md
```

Move with {{< kbd Space >}} and `b`, search with `/finished` and
{{< kbd Enter >}}, and quit with `q` (@tbl-less-keys). These are the keys
you used in `man` in @sec-getting-help, because `man` shows its pages
with `less`.

: Keys in `less` (and in `man`). {#tbl-less-keys}

| Key | Action |
|:----|:-------|
| {{< kbd Space >}} / `b` | one page forward / back |
| {{< kbd Down >}} / {{< kbd Up >}} | one line forward / back |
| `g` / `G` | start / end of the file |
| `/word` then {{< kbd Enter >}} | search forward for `word` |
| `n` / `N` | next / previous match |
| `-S` then {{< kbd Enter >}} | chop long lines instead of wrapping them (also `less -S file`) |
| `-N` then {{< kbd Enter >}} | show line numbers (also `less -N file`) |
| `q` | quit |

`less -S` keeps each line of a wide table on one screen line; scroll
sideways with the arrow keys. You will want it for wide tables and SAM
files (@sec-sam-bam-cram).

**What kind of file is it?** Before you `cat` something, `file` tells
you:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
file data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/meta/samples.tsv data/raw data/ref
```

```{.console}
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: gzip compressed data, last modified: Mon Apr 12 16:55:05 2021, from Unix, original size modulo 2^32 12776642
data/meta/samples.tsv:          ASCII text
data/raw:                       directory
data/ref:                       symbolic link to /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
```

`file` looks at the content, not the name: a `.txt` that is really
compressed would show as gzip. (On a Mac, `file` follows the link and
says `directory` for `data/ref`.) The FASTQ file is compressed, about
12.8 MB of text in 2.2 MB: `cat` on it prints binary noise, which can
garble the terminal (type `reset` and press {{< kbd Enter >}}, or close
the tab). Read compressed text with `zless`, which comes with gzip, or
with `gunzip -c … | head`, as in @sec-orientation:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 4
zless data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFBFFFFFFF
```

One read, four lines (@sec-fasta-fastq explains them). `zless` opens
the same file in `less`; quit with `q`. On some Linux systems plain
`less` also opens `.gz` files, because of a helper set up for it (Nova
has one); on others, including a Mac, it shows noise. Do not rely on it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `cat` on a compressed or binary file
It floods the terminal with noise and can leave it garbled. Check with
`file` first; read compressed text with `zless` or
`gunzip -c … | head`.
:::

**Two more.** `tail -f` follows a file as it grows, printing new lines
as they arrive, until you press {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}}: you will watch cluster
job logs this way (@sec-hpc-slurm). `wc -l` counts lines, as in
@sec-orientation, and `head -c` cuts by bytes, as in
@sec-getting-help's truncated copy.

**Editor or viewer?** Open a file in VS Code (`code file`,
@sec-book-setup) when you want to edit it. To look, use `head` or
`less`: an editor may try to load the whole file at the start, and a
5 GB file can freeze it. `head` reads only the start; `less` loads more
as you move, though searching or jumping to the end (`G`) can still read
most of the file, and paging through a decompressed stream is slower
than through a plain file.

: Ways to look inside a file. {#tbl-viewers}

| Command | Best for | Reads the whole file? | Works on `.gz`? |
|:--------|:---------|:----------------------|:----------------|
| `cat f` | short files | yes, and prints it all | no: noise |
| `head -n 5 f` | the first lines, column names | no | no; use `gunzip -c f \| head` |
| `tail -n 5 f` | the last lines, the end of a log | no | no |
| `tail -f f` | a log that is still growing | follows new lines | no |
| `less f` | browsing, searching | as far as you move | on some systems |
| `zless f` | browsing compressed text | as far as you move | yes |
| `file f` | what kind of file it is | no, only the start | yes: says `gzip compressed data` |
| `wc -l f` | counting lines | yes | no; `gunzip -c f \| wc -l` |

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "To see what is in a file, I open it in an editor"
**Reality.** Large files can freeze an editor, and compressed ones show
noise. `head`, `less`, and `file` let you look without loading the
whole file; `zless` and `gunzip -c … | head` read compressed text.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A colleague's 4 GB `counts.tsv` freezes their
editor. How do you see the column names and the first rows?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`head -n 5 counts.tsv`, which reads only the start. Or browse with
`less -S counts.tsv`, which does not load the whole file at the start
and keeps wide rows on one line.
:::
:::

## History and shortcuts {#sec-shell-basics-history}

Bash remembers what you type. Press {{< kbd Up >}} a few times: earlier
commands come back, ready to run with {{< kbd Enter >}} or to edit
first. To see a numbered list of recent ones:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
history | tail
```

(The `|` passes the list to `tail`, which keeps the last 10;
@sec-text-tools explains it.) Faster for an old command is **reverse
search**: press {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}} and type `seqkit`. The prompt changes
to `(reverse-i-search)` and shows the newest command containing
`seqkit`. Press {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}} again for older matches,
{{< kbd Enter >}} to run the one shown, or {{< kbd Right >}} (or
{{< kbd Esc >}}) to put it on the line to edit first.

**Editing a recalled line** without the arrow keys (@tbl-shortcuts):
jump to the start or end, move a word at a time, delete a word. The
most useful one for this chapter's habit is {{< kbd Alt-. >}}, which
inserts the last argument of the previous command. Preview with
`ls -d -- run2/*.tmp`, then type `rm -i -- ` and press
{{< kbd Alt-. >}}: the same pattern appears, without retyping it.

: Keys for history and line editing. {#tbl-shortcuts}

| Keys | Action | macOS note |
|:-----|:-------|:-----------|
| {{< kbd Up >}} / {{< kbd Down >}} | earlier / later command | |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}} | search history; again for older matches | |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} / {{< kbd Ctrl-E >}} | start / end of the line | |
| {{< kbd Alt-B >}} / {{< kbd Alt-F >}} | back / forward one word | needs Option as Meta (below) |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-W >}} | delete the word before the cursor | |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-U >}} / {{< kbd Ctrl-K >}} | delete to the start / to the end of the line | |
| {{< kbd Alt-. >}} | insert the last argument of the previous command | needs Option as Meta |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} | cancel the line, or stop a running program | |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-D >}} | end input; at an empty prompt, close the shell | |
| {{< kbd Ctrl-L >}} | clear the screen | |
| {{< kbd Tab >}} | complete; twice to list choices | |

{{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} stops a running program; stopping and managing
programs properly (processes, {{< kbd Ctrl-Z >}}, `kill`) is
@sec-linux-system. {{< kbd Ctrl-D >}} at an empty prompt closes the
shell: on a cluster that logs you out, so press it with care.

On a Mac, the {{< kbd Alt >}} keys need the Option key to act as Meta:
in Terminal, *Settings → Profiles → Keyboard → Use Option as Meta key*;
in iTerm2, *Settings → Profiles → Keys*, Left Option key: *Esc+*. VS
Code's built-in terminal may keep some shortcuts for itself.

You may also see `!!` (run the previous command again) and `!$` (its
last argument) in other people's notes. They run without showing you the
command first, so this book does not use them.

**Where history lives.** Bash keeps it in `~/.bash_history`. Each shell
normally loads that file when it starts and saves its own commands when
it exits, so a terminal that is already open will not show commands
typed in another one, even after that one is closed; a new terminal
will. Anything you type on
the command line is stored there, so never put a password or a token in
a command (@sec-getting-help). How much history is kept is a setting in
`~/.bashrc` (@sec-linux-system).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Search, don't scroll
{{< kbd Ctrl-R >}} finds an old command by any part of it, and
{{< kbd Alt-. >}} inserts the last argument of the previous one.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Name two ways to rerun yesterday's `seqkit stats`
command without retyping it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Press {{< kbd Up >}} until it appears; or press {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}} and
type `seqkit`. (`history | tail` and copying also works.)
:::
:::

## Summary {#sec-shell-basics-summary}

- Before a program starts, bash reads the line into words (respecting
  quotes), expands `~`, wildcards, and `$…` where quoting allows, removes
  the quotes, and starts the command with the resulting arguments.
  Builtins such as `cd` are part of bash; most commands are programs.
- Paths are absolute (from `/` or `~`) or relative (from the current
  working directory, which `pwd` prints), even inside a script. `.` is
  here, `..` is up one, `cd -` goes back, `cd` goes home.
- `cp` and `mv` overwrite silently and `rm` has no undo: preview with
  `ls -d --`, then use `-i`. A relative link target is read from the
  link's own folder; remove links with `unlink`, no trailing slash.
- An unquoted wildcard is matched by bash, each name one argument; no
  match passes the pattern on unchanged. Quote names with spaces, and
  quote patterns meant for the program, such as `find -name "*.fq.gz"`.
  Tab completes names and catches typos. Lowercase names without
  spaces or special characters need none of this care.
- `find <where> <tests>` finds files by name, type, depth, size, and
  age. `head`, `tail`, `less`, and `file` look inside files without
  loading them whole; `zless` reads compressed text. {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}}
  and the editing keys bring back and fix earlier commands.

: The chapter's commands on one page. {#tbl-ch05-commands}

| Task | Command |
|:-----|:--------|
| Where am I? Go somewhere | `pwd`, `cd path`, `cd ..`, `cd -`, `cd` |
| List | `ls`, `ls -lh`, `ls -a`, `ls -t`, `ls -d -- names` |
| Make | `mkdir -p a/b`, `touch file` |
| Copy, move, rename | `cp -i a b`, `cp -r dir dir2`, `mv -i old new` |
| Delete | `ls -d -- names` first, then `rm -i -- names`; `rmdir dir` |
| Link | `ln -s /absolute/target name`, `readlink name`, `unlink name` |
| Show arguments | `printf '<%s>\n' pattern` |
| Find | `find dir -type f -name "*.fastq.gz"`, `find dir -xtype l` |
| Look inside | `head -n 5`, `tail -n 5`, `less -S`, `zless`, `file`, `tail -f` |
| Recall | {{< kbd Up >}}, {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}}, {{< kbd Alt-. >}}, `history` |

## Exercises {#sec-shell-basics-exercises}

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Where am I?** Starting from `~`, reach
`~/bioinf-computing/data/raw` twice: once with one absolute path, once
with relative steps (one folder per `cd`). Then, from `data/raw` and
without `cd`, list `data/meta` and the reference folder through
`data/ref` using relative paths. Record each command in `NOTEBOOK.md`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`cd ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw` (or the path written out from `/`);
then `cd`, `cd bioinf-computing`, `cd data`, `cd raw`. From `data/raw`:
`ls ../meta` and `ls ../ref/` (the trailing slash lists the shared
folder's files through the link: `checksums.md5  genes.gtf.gz
genome.fa.gz  README.md`).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Predict the wildcard.** Do this before Exercise 3, which
changes the folder. In `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share`, write down what
each line prints, then run them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
echo */*_R1*
echo run?/*
echo */*.f*q.gz
echo *.bam
echo .*
echo run[!1]/*
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.console}
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
*.bam
.old_settings
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
```

Points to check: `*_R1*` also catches the `.tmp` copy; `*.f*q.gz`
matches both `.fastq.gz` and `.fq.gz` but not `.tmp`, because the name
must **end** in `q.gz`; `*/` searches one level of subfolders, including
the one with spaces; `*.bam` matched nothing and came out unchanged;
`run?` does not match `Run 3 final`, because case matters and `?` is one
character. The order follows your system's sorting rules and may
differ slightly.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. Tidy a lab share.** You inherit `share/` and want a clean
folder of read files to work from, without moving or copying the
originals.

1. From `~/bioinf-computing-ch05`, use `find` to list every read file,
   both `.fastq.gz` and `.fq.gz`, including those in the folder with
   spaces.
2. Make `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq/` and, from inside it, link
   each read file there **with an absolute target**, renaming `.fq.gz`
   to `.fastq.gz` so all six names are consistent. Two links, given
   complete; adapt them for the other four:

   ```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
   mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
   cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
   ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz .
   ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/"Run 3 final"/sample_C_R1.fq.gz sample_C_R1.fastq.gz
   ```

   (With `.` as the name, the link takes the target's own name.)
3. In `share`, remove the broken link `ref` with `unlink` (no slash),
   and delete the leftover `.tmp` file: preview with
   `ls -d -- run2/*.tmp`, then `rm -i -- run2/*.tmp`.
4. Check, with these four commands (the `| sort` puts the lines in
   order; @sec-text-tools):

   ```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
   find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy -type l -printf '%f -> %l\n' | sort
   find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy -xtype l
   find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy -type f
   find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share \( -xtype l -o -name '*.tmp' \) -print
   ```

   The first lists each link and its target (`%f` the link's name, `%l`
   the stored target); the second lists broken links; the third,
   ordinary files that should not be in `tidy`; the fourth, a broken
   link or `.tmp` file left in `share`. Only the first should print
   anything.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05
find share -type f \( -name "*.fastq.gz" -o -name "*.fq.gz" \)
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/"Run 3 final"/sample_C_R1.fq.gz sample_C_R1.fastq.gz
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/"Run 3 final"/sample_C_R2.fq.gz sample_C_R2.fastq.gz
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
unlink ref
ls -d -- run2/*.tmp
rm -i -- run2/*.tmp
```

The first check prints these six lines, with your own home folder in
place of `/home/you` (compare everything after it):

```{.console}
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
sample_A_R2.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
sample_B_R2.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
sample_C_R1.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
sample_C_R2.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
```

The other three print nothing. Six working links that all point to the
same file would pass the second check but not the first, which is why
the first lists every target. Read a link to be sure it works:
`gunzip -c sample_C_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 4` in `tidy/fastq` prints
the first record, `@C.1`.

The most common mistake is a relative target, such as
`ln -s run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq/`
run from `share`: the link stores `run1/…`, which is read from
`tidy/fastq/`, and the second check lists it as broken. Remove it with
`unlink` and make it again with the absolute path.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Read a log without opening it.** In `~/bioinf-computing`,
list the logs newest first with `ls -t logs`. Find the newest log of a
run that **finished**: @sec-getting-help made a run fail on purpose, and
its log, probably the newest, has no `finished:` line. Check each
candidate with `tail -n 3`. In the finished log, show the first 3 lines
with `head`, then open it in `less` and use `/finished` to jump to the
last line. Which seqkit version did the run use?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The failed run's log ends with the `md5sum` lines, with no `finished:`.
A finished log ends like this (the book's, from @sec-organizing-projects):

```{.console}
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
```

The version is on the `seqkit:` line, in the first lines `head -n 5`
shows: `seqkit v2.14.0` in the book's log. If you have no log at all,
read the book's in @sec-organizing-projects and rerun the script there
when you can.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5. Peek into compressed data.** Run `file` on
`data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz` and `data/ref/genes.gtf.gz`. Look at
the first read with `zless`, and at the first two lines of the
annotation with `gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | head -n 2`. The first
column of a GTF line names the chromosome. Which chromosome does each
of the two lines name? Note what you find in `NOTEBOOK.md`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`file` says `gzip compressed data` for both. The first GTF line names
`not_in_genome`, and the second `I`:

```{.console}
not_in_genome	ensembl	CDS	335	646	.	+	0	exon_number "1"; gene_biotype "protein_coding"; …
I	ensembl	exon	335	649	.	+	.	exon_id "YAL069W.1"; exon_number "1"; …
```

(Lines shortened here at `…`.) The genome file has one sequence, `I`,
so the first line describes a chromosome that is not in the genome.
This is a test file, and an odd line like this one tests how tools cope;
of the file's 600 lines, all the others are on `I`. Looking at the
start of a file is how you catch such things before a tool does. GTF is
@sec-intervals-variants.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 6. History drill.** Using only {{< kbd Ctrl-R >}} and the
editing keys, recall Exercise 4's `head` command and change it to `tail`
without retyping the log's name.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
{{< kbd Ctrl-R >}}, type `head -n`, then {{< kbd Right >}} to edit;
{{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} to jump to the start, {{< kbd Alt-F >}} past `head`,
{{< kbd Ctrl-W >}} to delete it, type `tail`, {{< kbd Enter >}}. Other
key sequences work as well; the point is not to retype the path.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-shell-basics-reading}

- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, chapters 2–5 and 7
  (navigation, exploring the system, manipulating files, "Seeing the
  world as the shell sees it") --- the same ground as this chapter,
  slower and with more examples; free online.
- @wilson2019swcarpentry, Software Carpentry's [*The Unix
  Shell*](https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/), episodes on
  navigating, working with files, and finding things --- short lessons
  with exercises, written for researchers.
- @ramey2025bash, the [*Bash Reference
  Manual*](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/), sections *Shell
  Expansions* and *Quoting* --- the exact rules behind
  @fig-shell-steps, for when you want the whole story.
- @gnu2025findutils, the [GNU findutils
  manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/manual/)
  --- every `find` test and action, including the safe use of `-exec`
  and `-delete` for later.
